notes.meaning: Moses describes a situation where an unhappy marriage ends in divorce and the woman later remarries. Under this civil rule, a husband could not simply banish his wife with an angry word; he had to give her a formal written certificate that legally ended the marriage and protected her right to marry again. Moses was not creating or commanding divorce here, but regulating an existing practice to restrain sudden breakups and protect women from unfair treatment.

If the woman's second marriage ends through divorce or the death of her husband, the first husband is strictly forbidden from ever marrying her again. Taking her back after she had lived with another man is treated here as a defilement and an offensive practice that would corrupt the promised land. This strict rule forced husbands to think carefully before putting away a wife, knowing that the decision was permanent and could never be reversed.

differ.view: Many in this tradition hold that divorce and remarriage are permissible only for sexual unfaithfulness or desertion, understanding Moses' law as a civil concession to human sinfulness rather than God's ideal design.
Some teach that because marriage makes two people one flesh, Scripture forbids all remarriage after divorce while both original spouses are still living.

notes.meaning: A newly married man was completely excused from military service and public duties for one full year. This command gave husband and wife dedicated time at home to build strong bonds of affection, adjust to each other, and bring joy into their new household. Guarding the warmth and unity of the home early on helped prevent future misunderstandings and marital breakdown.

Creditors were forbidden to take handmill stones as security or collateral for a debt. Ancient families relied on these stones every morning to grind grain into flour for daily bread, so seizing either stone meant depriving them of their meals. God's law taught lenders that securing money must never destroy another person's ability to feed their family.

Kidnapping a fellow Israelite to enslave or sell them was treated as a capital crime punishable by death. Stolen property could be paid back, but stealing a human being stripped away a person's God-given freedom and dignity. Executing the kidnapper removed a dangerous evil from the community and warned everyone that human lives must never be bought and sold.

The people were commanded to follow the instructions of the Levitical priests carefully whenever contagious skin diseases broke out. Moses reminded them of Miriam, who was struck with such a disease and quarantined outside the camp when she challenged his leadership. This warning showed that God's health and purity laws applied equally to all, with no special exceptions made for wealth or high rank.

A person lending money or goods was forbidden to enter the borrower's house to take a pledge for the loan. Instead, the lender had to wait outside while the borrower selected and brought out an item he could afford to spare. This rule protected the privacy, dignity, and peace of a struggling family, keeping aggressive lenders from seizing household necessities.

If a poor person gave their outer cloak as a loan guarantee, the lender had to return it every evening before sunset. In that climate, the poor often had only one heavy garment that also served as their sleeping blanket at night. Returning the coat ensured the poor man did not suffer in the cold, invited his grateful prayers, and was counted by God as genuine righteousness.

Employers were commanded never to mistreat poor workers, whether fellow Israelites or resident foreigners, by delaying their daily wages. A day laborer lived hand to mouth and relied entirely on each day's pay to buy food for his family that evening. Holding back wages was a grave injustice, and God promised to hear and avenge the cry of the unpaid worker.

Human courts were forbidden to execute parents for the crimes of their children, or children for the sins of their parents. Unlike neighboring nations that often put entire families to death for treason, Israel's courts were required to hold each individual accountable only for their own deeds. True justice protects innocent relatives from cruel vengeance.

Judges and neighbors were required to treat foreigners, orphans, and widows with absolute fairness. A lender was specifically barred from ever taking a widow's cloak as a debt pledge, since she had no husband to advocate for her. Israel was reminded that they were once mistreated slaves in Egypt whom the Lord redeemed, so they ought to show that same compassion to others.

When farmers harvested grain and accidentally left a sheaf behind in the field, they were not allowed to go back and retrieve it. That forgotten food was set aside for foreigners, orphans, and widows who owned no land of their own. Allowing the needy to glean allowed them to feed themselves through honest labor, and the Lord promised to bless the generous landowner.

The same rule of generous sharing applied to olive groves and vineyards after the primary harvest was gathered. Owners were told not to strip their branches or vines bare with a second pass, but to leave whatever remained behind for the poor. This arrangement ensured that vulnerable families could enjoy nutritious food and fruit without having to beg.

Moses repeated the reminder that Israel had lived as poor, oppressed slaves in Egypt before God rescued them. Keeping their own painful history fresh in mind helped them treat the destitute with generosity rather than arrogance. Remembering God's great mercy toward us is the strongest motivation to care for those in need.
